reviewerOrPass: Worker A, same AI, separate source-first pass
method: After freezing and replaying the pair, returned to the programme-specific 2026–27 regulations, separately reconciled the three 60 EC tables and compared Article 8.1 against the current public programme. Re-read the compulsory-order table and then reconsidered the U.S. anchors, methods and limitations of the three plans from the current workbook. Checked each displayed alignment against shared course content or method. This was a separate same-AI pass.
findings: The English-taught BA comprises 60 EC each year. The 2026-entry structure in Arts. 4.1 and 5.1 assigns Stories We Live By to year one, North & South Americans to year two alongside three 10 EC courses and four rotating 5 EC topics, and a 30 EC minor, 10 EC research seminar, 10 EC faculty-wide course and 10 EC thesis to year three. The public overview places Stories We Live By in both years one and two and names Mobility, Migration, Transculturation instead of the year-three Research Seminar. The repeat of Stories and the year-three title align with elements of the 2025-entry transition in Art. 8.1. The illustrated 2026-entry case therefore uses the formal names and credit structure. Named rotating topics on the public page are examples. The first 10 EC faculty-wide course is prescribed; the second is a choice among published themes. The minor may be fulfilled through eligible choices including study abroad.

Article 7.1 requires The Americas I or II before Americas III and Practice I before Practice II. The study-abroad choice requires the first year, Practice II and 30 additional second-year EC. The Research Seminar requires the first year and Practice II. The thesis requires the first year and Practice II plus 10 EC in Theories of Culture II or The Americas III. The older numbered subdivisions in the progression text are interpreted within the current course structure. No seminar-before-thesis requirement is inferred from the article.

The broad plan connects Native American and gender histories, American media and race, comparative politics, and historical inquiry to broader social and cultural context. The media and culture plan builds from narrative and film to media technologies, adaptation, creative work and documentary, with an American anchor in media, race and gender history. The politics plan centers on comparative institutions, empire, international relations and law, rights and conflict, with the U.S. anchor supplied by historical study and the media courses. Introductory courses precede qualifying and advanced work in all three. The case distinguishes a substantive point of overlap from a complementary course. The six aligned rows support concrete common domains or methods. General economics, literary study and creative production do not carry a designated comparator match. Comparable work in migration, inequality and political economy does not supply sustained Canada and Latin America coursework, and recycling that material would not create a distinct fourth plan.
